lessons.title: Enterprise budgets and gross margins
lessons.html:
Budgeting as a planning tool

A budget is a financial plan expressed in rand. At N5 level, budgets are used to compare enterprises, test changes before making them and control the business during the year. The main types are enterprise budgets, partial budgets, whole-farm budgets and cash flow budgets.

Fixed and variable costs

  • Variable (directly allocatable) costs change with the size of an enterprise and can be linked to it: seed, fertiliser, chemicals, feed, veterinary costs, fuel for that crop, casual labour, marketing costs.
  • Fixed (overhead) costs do not change much with the size of any one enterprise in the short term: permanent wages, insurance, depreciation, office costs, interest on long-term debt.

Gross margin

The gross margin of an enterprise = gross production value minus directly allocatable variable costs. It is usually expressed per hectare or per animal unit, so enterprises can be compared.

Dryland maize, per hectareAmount
Expected yield 5 t at R3,800 per tR19,000
SeedR3,200
FertiliserR5,100
Herbicides and pesticidesR1,900
Fuel, repairs and contract workR2,600
Insurance and marketingR1,200
Total variable costsR14,000
Gross marginR5,000 per ha

The gross margin must cover the farm's fixed costs and leave a profit. A positive gross margin alone does not mean the farm is profitable.

Sensitivity analysis

Because yields and prices vary, test the budget at different values. At 4 t/ha and the same costs the gross margin drops to R1,200 per ha; at R3,400 per t and 5 t/ha it is R3,000. A break-even yield (variable costs divided by price) of about 3.7 t/ha tells the manager how much risk the enterprise carries.

lessons.title: Partial, whole-farm and cash flow budgets
lessons.html:
Partial budgets

A partial budget evaluates a specific change, such as buying a planter instead of using a contractor, or replacing 50 ha of maize with soya. Only the items that change are included:

Positive effectsNegative effects
Additional incomeIncome lost
Costs savedAdditional costs

If total positive effects exceed total negative effects, the change improves profit, provided the risk and the impact on cash flow are acceptable. Non-financial factors such as timeliness, labour and management time should also be noted.

The whole-farm budget

The whole-farm budget combines the gross margins of all planned enterprises and subtracts fixed costs to estimate net farm income for the year. It is used to test the overall farm plan and is often required by lenders.

The cash flow budget

A cash flow budget shows expected cash in and cash out per month for the coming year. It answers a different question from the profit budget: will the business have enough cash at each point in time?

  1. Start with the opening bank balance.
  2. For each month, list expected cash receipts: crop and livestock sales, loans received, other income.
  3. List expected cash payments: inputs, wages, fuel, repairs, loan instalments, tax, personal drawings, capital purchases.
  4. Net cash flow = receipts minus payments; closing balance = opening balance plus net cash flow, carried to the next month.

Months with negative balances show when overdraft or production credit is needed. In summer grain areas, large outflows occur at planting (October to December) while income arrives after harvest (May to August).

Budget control

Compare actual figures with budget monthly. Investigate significant variances: was the price lower, the yield lower or a cost item overspent? Act early and update forecasts.

Key points

  • Gross margin = gross production value minus variable costs.
  • Gross margins must cover fixed costs before there is profit.
  • Use sensitivity and break-even analysis to understand risk.
  • Partial budgets evaluate a specific change using only items that change.
  • Cash flow budgets show monthly cash needs; compare actuals with budget regularly.
